You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Below are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

=== TRANSCRIPTS ===
# Interview — a fleet technician

Interviewer: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start until you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. Think of yesterday: what was the first thing you did when you got to work?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem. Is there something about these questions that makes them hard to answer?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's try something smaller. What is the last drone you touched at work, and what did you do to it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Has anything gone badly at work in the last few months that stuck in your mind?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order by adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at my company's sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Regulators can ask my company to show how its drones have been looked after, and repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians.

Interviewer: Thank you, that helps. When did you last take a drone out of service, and what happened from start to finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned regulators can ask how drones have been looked after. What do they ask to see?

Interviewee: Regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians.

Interviewer: Who gives you work, or tells you something needs doing?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When a drone needs to go and charge, how is that decided?

Interviewee: I send drones to charge as part of keeping the drones and charging equipment in working order. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: Is there anything you double-check yourself because you don't fully trust it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Setting up charging pads at a site: what does that involve?

Interviewee: I set up charging pads at my company's sites. Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, a few dozen of them.

Interviewer: What would worry you about a new shared service handling your drones and charging pads?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order by adding new drones, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: When a charging pad or a drone stops working, what is the first thing you need to find out?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you retire an old drone, what happens next?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order by retiring old ones. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: How do you know a repaired drone is ready to go back into service?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Do you ever have anything to do with the other drone companies or their equipment?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you take a drone out of service, who needs to know?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When a new drone arrives, what do you do before it can fly jobs?

Interviewee: I add new drones to the fleet to keep the drones and charging equipment in working order. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: Where is the record of a drone's repairs and servicing kept today?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What is the most frustrating part of your job?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Has sending a drone to charge ever gone wrong?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You said repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians. Is that you, or other people?

Interviewee: Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and I keep drones and charging equipment in working order. Regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after. I don't know any further details.

Interviewer: Is there anything else about your work that you think I should know?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order by adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at my company's sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians. Regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.

---

# Interview — a dispatcher

Interviewer: Can you walk me through an ordinary working day, from the moment you start?

Interviewee: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I plan and run the flights. I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can call off a flight, and several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones.

Interviewer: What is the very first thing you do when you start your shift?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Think of your last shift. What did you look at or open first that morning?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you sign off a flight before it leaves, what do you check?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned several dispatchers plan at the same time for the same sites and drones. What happens when two of you want the same drone?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What was the worst day you've had in the last few months?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When did you last call off a flight, and why?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who gives you the work you plan each day?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there something that makes these questions hard to answer?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you check by hand today because you don't trust it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What worries you most about a new service being brought in for your work?

Interviewee: I worry about closures coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on, and batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time a closure came into force while one of your drones was already in the air. What happened?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When a closure comes in while drones are flying, what are you afraid a new service would get wrong?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Right after something has gone wrong with a flight, what do you need to know first?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When reports from a drone arrive late or not at all, how do you find out where it actually is?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you do when you learn a drone has restarted in flight?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who do you hand a flight over to when you can't finish it yourself?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When a battery drains faster than planned, what happens next?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How do you hear about a new closure today?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What does the end of your shift look like?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When drones from other companies are flying near yours, what do you need to know about them?

Interviewee: I know that airspace information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone, and authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned and sudden closures. My notes do not state what I need to know about drones from other companies when they are flying near mine.

Interviewer: When a sudden closure is announced, what do you do in the first few minutes?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who do you contact first when something goes wrong during a flight?

Interviewee: I don't know.

---

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

Interviewer: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start until you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. Let's take yesterday: what was the first thing you did when you started work?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's step back. In your own words, what is your job on the airspace desk?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace. This involves handling the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: When a closure is announced by the authorities, what happens from the moment you hear about it?

Interviewee: The authorities announce closures, which can be planned ones with a start and end time, or sudden ones that apply at once. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. Closures are often amended during the day, for example when an area is widened or an end time moves.

Interviewer: Can you tell me about the most recent closure you handled, step by step?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You said you want to know how much disruption a closure caused across customers. What does "disruption" mean to you in that case?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What was the worst day you've had in the last few months?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything you currently check by hand because you don't fully trust it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned closures are often amended during the day, like an area being widened. What do you have to do when that happens?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who do you get work from, and who do you pass work on to?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What would worry you most about a new service handling the airspace picture?

Interviewee: The service runs on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and it occasionally crashes. The companies accept a few minutes of interruption, which worries me given that closures can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.

Interviewer: What would happen if a sudden closure came in during one of those few minutes when the service is down?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Right after a sudden closure comes into force while drones are in the air, what is the first thing you need to know?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you look at how a closure affected the different customer companies, what are you allowed to see about each company's flights or jobs?

Interviewee: I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business.

Interviewer: Then how do you find out how much disruption a closure caused, if you can't look into any one company's operations?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned the network of flight corridors and the zones that group them. When does that network change?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who enters a closure into the system today?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you do with the information about how much disruption a closure caused?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Has the current system ever crashed or restarted while you were entering or changing a closure?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What mistakes have you seen happen with closures?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How is your work different for a planned closure compared with a sudden one?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What information do the authorities give you when they announce a closure?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who at the customer companies do you talk to, if anyone?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything else about your work that you think I should know?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, including the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
=== END OF TRANSCRIPTS ===

Write the requirements for the service: what it must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does. Rest every requirement on what the interviews say.

Write them as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, and nothing else:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
